questions.text: We got a panic in production that says `deleted more than stored` — what does that mean and what would cause it?
questions.how_found: Grepped the panic string; it fires in UsagePool.Delete when the reference count goes below zero. Read the method doc (lines 166-170) and the UsagePool type doc at the top of the same file, which spells out the invariant: Delete must be called exactly as many times as LoadOrStore/LoadOrNew.
questions.why_asked: A newcomer hitting an unfamiliar panic in the logs needs to know which internal invariant was violated and whether it is their plugin's fault (unbalanced Delete) rather than a core bug.

questions.text: Caddy refuses to start with `probe resistance requires authentication` — what does the forward proxy want me to configure?
questions.how_found: Grepped the error string; it is returned from Handler.Provision when ProbeResistance is set but AuthCredentials is nil. The adjacent lines also show that a configured secret domain is logged at INFO on startup, and caddyfile.go's `basic_auth` case is what populates AuthCredentials.
questions.why_asked: A config-time fatal error is the first thing a new operator meets; they need to know which directive is missing rather than guessing.

questions.text: Our TLS logs are full of `subject name does not qualify for certificate` — what check produces that, and which names does it reject?
questions.how_found: Grepped the message to checkIfCertShouldBeObtained in handshake.go, then followed SubjectQualifiesForCert into certificates.go:593-613 (empty names, leading/trailing dots, non-leftmost wildcards, and a set of accidental special characters are all rejected). The same function also shows the other two rejection paths: no OnDemand config at all, and the DecisionFunc / hostAllowlist checks.
questions.why_asked: On-demand TLS silently failing for some SNI values is a classic first-week support ticket; you need to know exactly which names are filtered out before blaming the ACME CA.

questions.text: Our CI publishes xcaddy build output and I see `[REDACTED]` in it — what puts that there, and how do we choose what gets masked?
questions.how_found: Grepped the literal; redactedPlaceholder is defined in redact.go and substituted by redactRule.apply, either for exact secrets or for the builtinCredentialRules (URL userinfo, GitHub/GitLab/Slack tokens, AWS key IDs) plus PEM private-key blocks. The knobs are Builder.Secrets and Builder.RedactCredentials, documented at builder.go:105-121 and wired in Build via configureRedaction at builder.go:351; both are no-ops unless OnStep is set.
questions.why_asked: Seeing masked text in a build log raises two immediate questions for a new engineer: is the masking trustworthy, and can I add our own secrets to it?

questions.text: The builder image sets `XCADDY_SETCAP=1` — what does that actually do to the binary it produces, and does it need elevated privileges?
questions.how_found: The variable is only declared in caddy-docker (Dockerfile.builder.tmpl:15 and the rendered 2.11/builder/Dockerfile), with a one-line comment. The behaviour lives in xcaddy: setcapIfRequested runs `setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep <output>` on the freshly built binary, wrapping it in `sudo` unless sudo is missing or XCADDY_SUDO=0.
questions.why_asked: Someone editing the Docker builder image sees an env var whose effect is not implemented anywhere in that repo, and needs to know whether it will demand a password or fail in a rootless build.

questions.text: Our certificate Secrets have mangled names — a `*` turns into `wildcard_` and a `:` into `-`. Is our Kubernetes storage adapter doing that, or something upstream?
questions.how_found: Started in the obvious place, ingress/pkg/storage/storage.go, whose cleanKey only collapses characters Kubernetes names disallow into '.' and prepends 'caddy.ingress--'. It never touches '*'. The asterisk-to-wildcard_ and ':'-to-'-' substitutions happen one layer up, in certmagic's KeyBuilder.Safe, which builds the storage key before any Storage implementation sees it (see CertsSitePrefix/SiteCert at storage.go:229-246).
questions.why_asked: Debugging a missing certificate starts with `kubectl get secrets`, and the names do not match the domains; you need to know which layer owns the naming scheme before you can predict a key.

questions.text: Our controller only accepts requests over TLS by default — where does that restriction come from, and can it be turned off for a single service?
questions.how_found: Traced the generated config: global/ingress.go builds one route per Ingress path and runs every IngressMiddleware over it; MatcherPlugin is the one that populates the matcher set, and it unconditionally adds a `protocol: https` condition unless the `caddy.ingress.kubernetes.io/disable-ssl-redirect` annotation (constant at internal/caddy/ingress/annotations.go:9) is exactly "true".
questions.why_asked: A first deployment where cleartext traffic does not behave as expected is very common, and the per-Ingress escape hatch is not discoverable from the generated JSON.

questions.text: Is there a built-in keyword covering the usual LAN and loopback networks that I can drop into a trusted-proxy directive, and does it include IPv6 link-local?
questions.how_found: Found the token handling in modules/caddyhttp/ip_range.go:95, modules/caddyhttp/ip_matchers.go:82/195, modules/caddyhttp/reverseproxy/caddyfile.go:708 and modules/caddytls/matchers.go:417/525 — all of them expand the same shortcut into internal.PrivateRangesCIDR(). The list itself is only nine lines: 192.168/16, 172.16/12, 10/8, 127.0.0.1/8, fd00::/8 and ::1. IPv6 link-local (fe80::/10) is NOT in it — unlike certmagic's isInternalIP (certificates.go:658-669) and forwardproxy's built-in deny list (forwardproxy.go:155-168), which both include fe80::/10. Note also that the IPv4 loopback entry is written 127.0.0.1/8 rather than 127.0.0.0/8.
questions.why_asked: Getting the trusted-proxy set wrong is a client-IP spoofing bug; before copying the shortcut into production you want to see the exact list and its gaps.

questions.text: Some of our rules use a terse `{...}` notation and others a much longer dotted one for the same thing — what expands the terse form, and is there a complete table of the abbreviations?
questions.how_found: Read the httpcaddyfile package: NewShorthandReplacer builds a strings.Replacer from placeholderShorthands() (a flat old/new pair list of ~36 entries) plus a dozen regexp rules for the parameterised ones ({header.X}, {query.X}, {re.X}, {rp.X}, ...). ApplyToSegment rewrites every token's text, so by the time a directive is unmarshalled only the long dotted form exists.
questions.why_asked: Reading an unfamiliar config, you constantly hit tokens that are not documented next to the directive that uses them, and you want the one authoritative list rather than guessing.

questions.text: Do I hand-edit the image recipes under each version folder, or are they produced from something else — and what produces them?
questions.how_found: The default goal is gen-dockerfiles, which runs gomplate over render-dockerfiles.tmpl with the five *.tmpl bodies and stackbrew-config.yaml as data, plus a getChecksums.sh plugin that pulls per-architecture SHA-512 sums from the tagged GitHub release. So everything under 2.11/*/ is output, and the per-variant Dockerfile.base files plus the top-level templates are the inputs. README.md:14-22 describes the same flow as the release procedure; library/caddy is produced by the second target.
questions.why_asked: The obvious move for a first change is to open the checked-in artifact and edit it; without knowing it is generated, your change gets silently overwritten on the next release.

questions.text: Our relay tells the destination who the original caller was — can we suppress it?
questions.how_found: Read Handler.ServeHTTP: unless the HideIP field (declared at forwardproxy.go:62) is set, it copies any inbound Forwarded / X-Forwarded-For headers and appends its own `Forwarded: for="<RemoteAddr>"` entry, stashing the result in the context for the upstream dial. The same flag is consulted again at line 354 on the CONNECT path. A sibling field, HideVia, controls the Via header separately.
questions.why_asked: Anyone running a proxy for privacy or compliance reasons has to know exactly what identifying data leaks downstream by default, and which switch stops it.

questions.text: If a pair of entries can each answer an incoming URL, what decides which one wins — and is that logic active out of the box?
questions.how_found: IngressSortPlugin runs with Priority -2, i.e. after all the per-Ingress routes have been generated, and reorders them with a stable sort: exact paths before prefix paths, longer before shorter within the same kind, empty paths last. Crucially the whole thing is gated on store.ConfigMap.ExperimentalSmartSort (declared at pkg/store/configmap_parser.go:20), so by default no reordering happens at all and the routes keep the order the Kubernetes objects were iterated in.
questions.why_asked: Two Ingresses with overlapping paths is a routine production situation; you need to know whether the platform resolves it deterministically for you or whether you must avoid the overlap yourself.
